opening.headline: The reason why the model misses instructions when long documents and questions are put in one lump is explained by the division and arrangement order of the input.
body: Let's say you pasted 20 pages of the contract and immediately followed it up with questions, summary instructions, and output format without line breaks. Even for a human to see, it is difficult to see where a contract ends and where a request begins. Models face the same challenges.

In this class, we will look at how to create boundaries between documents, instructions, examples, and questions using delimiters and XML tags, and the placement principle of placing questions at the top of long documents and at the end. At the end, we follow the process of designing the contract question and answer input structure from scratch.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the effects of delimiters, tags, and the arrangement order of long documents
You can differentiate between documents, questions, and instructions and how to place them.

screens.title: I put long documents and questions in one lump.
screens.lead: Read the input below and select the highlighted passages. Each passage explains what this input will look like to the model and where the problem may be.

visual.alt: An input box where the contract text, questions, instructions, and output format are connected without borders.

data.text: [Page 20 of the contract text] Article 1 Purpose Article 12 Termination of Contract Article 18 Other What are the termination conditions? Please summarize and organize it in a table. Please answer in JSON format

marks.note: This is the document area. Although it is the largest, there is no indication of where the document ends, making it difficult for the model to distinguish between the end of the document and the beginning of the request.

It's an actual question. The intention was to summarize only the termination terms, but since the questions are in one line with the document, it's easy for the responses to flow into a full summary of the contract.

marks.span: Please summarize and organize it in a table.
marks.note: This is an instruction. Because it is attached to the question, it is unclear whether it is part of the question or a separate instruction.
Output format request. The last sentence is easy to miss because it continues without boundaries between documents, questions, and instructions.

screens.outro: There are two candidate causes. The point is that there are no boundaries and questions are buried.

screens.title: In a long input, should the question be asked before or after?
screens.lead: As you select each batch, the instructor's thoughts unfold. This is not a time to choose a set answer, but to compare it with your habits, and you do not enter or submit it.

items.answer: If you write the question first, it seems natural because the model knows what to look for and starts reading. It also resembles human reading habits. However, if the document becomes very long, the point of writing the questions and answers at the beginning becomes distant. In the screens that follow, see how both guides address this issue.

The method is to show the material first and ask questions at the end. The question is placed right before the answer, which helps the model remember the request clearly. We go on to note that this arrangement is recommended for long inputs.

items.prompt: Either way, have you ever drawn a line between a document and a question?
items.answer: Boundaries are just as important as placement. The presence or absence of a single line or tag between a document and a question can significantly change the model's interpretation. Let’s look at these two elements separately: placement and border.

screens.outro: First, let's check how to create boundaries: delimiters and tags.

screens.title: Delimiters and XML tags: distinguishing types of content
screens.lead: Select the two states alternately and compare how the same content changes when it is divided into tags and without tags.

visual.alt: A side-by-side comparison of borderless input and input divided by tags.

states.label: no tags
states.body: This is a text where documents, instructions, and questions are connected without line breaks. You have to guess for yourself where the model ends with the data and where the work begins. If the material contains a sentence such as “summarize,” there is a risk that it may be misunderstood as an instruction. The input on the previous screen was in this state.

states.label: Has tag
states.body: A separator is a mark that divides sections, such as `---`, title, or markdown header. Claude's guide explains that when instructions, context, examples, and input are mixed, wrapping them in XML tags such as `<instructions>`, `<context>`, and `<input>` reduces misunderstandings. Several documents even separate their sources by putting `<document_content>` and `<source>` within `<document>`. Markdown headers and lists show the hierarchy of sections, and XML tags are great for demarcating content such as documents. Prompts can be easier to read if you divide them into roles, instructions, examples, and input and give them names.

screens.outro: Now that we've created the border, let's see what order we'll place the zones in.

screens.title: Location of long documents and questions
screens.lead: Each time you select the right arrow, one block will be stacked. Take a look at the recommendations from both guides and their common principles in order.

visual.alt: Blocks of documents, instructions and questions stacked from top to bottom.

steps.title: Claude Guide: Document to the Top
steps.body: Claude's guide recommends putting the document at the top of the prompt for long inputs of 20k tokens or more. Place questions, instructions, and examples below them. The first block is a long document.

steps.title: Gemini Guide: Questions at the End
steps.body: Gemini's Long Contexts article explains that when contexts are long, it usually performs better to place questions at the end of the prompt, i.e. after other contexts. Instructions and examples are placed in the second block, and questions are placed last.

steps.title: Common principles of both guides
steps.body: The expressions are different, but the direction is the same. Put longer material first and questions last. By following this order, questions are not buried in the document and the model encounters the request again just before writing the answer.

steps.title: Have them quote first
steps.body: Claude's guide tells you that when working on long documents, you can filter out unnecessary content by first citing the relevant parts and then working on them. If it is a contract, instruct them to cite the termination clause first and then respond.

steps.title: Placement is important even in large windows
steps.body: Gemini's 1M token context is equivalent to approximately 8 novels. Even with these large windows, it still matters what you put where. The fact that it goes in and the fact that it is read well are different.

screens.outro: Now that we know the principles, let's compare how the actual response changes when we change the arrangement.

screens.title: Example of different responses when changing placement
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare prompts and responses from three batches of the same model and contract, with only the input structure changed.

tabs.label: Batch 1
tabs.body:
**Structure:** Write the question first and attach it to the entire contract. There are no tags. Example: Page 20 of the contract body, starting from the line after “Just summarize the termination conditions.”

**Response:** Since the questions are so far removed from the document and have no boundaries, the response flows into a full summary of the contract. In fact, the requested cancellation conditions are mixed among various contents.

tabs.label: Batch 2
tabs.body:
**Structure:** Attach the contract first and place questions at the end. There are no tags.

**Response:** I do find a termination clause at the end of the question. However, there is no boundary between documents and sources, so article numbers are mixed. The location has improved, but the lack of boundaries remains.

tabs.label: Batch 3
tabs.body:
**Structure:** Enter the contract as `<document>` in `<documents>` and give the file name as `<source>`. In the instructions below, put `<question>` at the end.

**Response:** Only the termination clauses are listed with clause numbers. Because the document and question are separated and the question is at the end, the model gets exactly what it needs.

tabs.label: What was different?
tabs.body: The model, contract, and questions are the same for all three batches. The only thing that has changed is the structure of the input. The factors that made the difference can be summarized in two points. Firstly, whether the document and question are separated by tags, and secondly, whether the question is at the end. This comparison refers to the statement that the input structure determines the reading order of the model.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the principles, let's sort the pieces of input into the appropriate regions.

screens.title: Explanation: Classifying each part of the input separately
screens.lead: Read the table from top to bottom and follow where the instructor places each piece. The reasons in the last column are the criteria for judgment.

data.caption: Fragments and appropriate areas for entering contract questions and answers.
rows: This is because it is the data that the model will read and use as the basis for its answer.
This is because it is metadata that distinguishes which document the content comes from when there are multiple documents.
This is because it is a statement that determines how the model should work.
This is the core of this request, and it is clearest when placed right before writing the answer.
A pair of examples of what the output JSON looks like
This is because it is data showing the shape of the output and must be wrapped separately so as not to be mixed with the instructions.
data.notes: The key point is that the five pieces are divided into different areas. The text is the data, the file name is the information of the data, the citation request is an instruction, and the question is a request. The starting point for differentiation is the habit of first asking about the personality of each piece. For ambiguous pieces, you can ask whether the model reads them and uses them as the basis for an answer, or whether it accepts them as actions to be followed. If it's evidence, it's in the document or source, and if it's action, it's in the direction of instructions or questions. Unlike these two, the example is material that shows the format, so it must be wrapped separately.

screens.outro: Now that you've sorted the pieces, let's put them in order and assemble the entire structure.

screens.title: Explanation: Contract question and answer input structure design on page 20
screens.lead: Each time you select the right arrow, one area is added to the prompt. Follow the order in which the instructor assembles the inputs.

steps.title: Step 1 Document at the top
steps.body: Open `<documents>` at the top and enter the contract as `<document>`. Enter the file name as `<source>` and place the text in `<document_content>`. This arrangement follows the principle of putting longer documents first.

steps.title: Step 2 instructions below
steps.body: Below the document, write `<instructions>` and write "Cite the relevant clause first and then reply." If you ask for a quote first, the model will select only the relevant parts and then write an answer.

steps.title: Step 3 Output Shape Example
steps.body: Put a pair of output shapes as `<example>`. For example, here's one JSON containing the clause number and summary. Examples are divided into instructions and tags to avoid confusion.

steps.title: Step 4 questions at the end
steps.body: At the end, with `<question>`, “What are the conditions for termination?” Leave one line. The question is placed right before the answer so the model doesn't miss the point of the request.

steps.title: Step 5 Check the final structure
steps.body: The completed structure is a document, instructions, examples, and questions. Finally, check that the document, sources, instructions, examples, and questions are all separated by tags and that the question is at the end. Compared to the initial jumbled input, the order in which the model will read them becomes clear.

screens.outro: Now that we've completed the design process, let's close by summarizing the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Input Structure Determines Reading Order
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Check the answer to the question you asked at the beginning: whether the same model will follow instructions properly if you change its structure.

paragraphs: To answer your initial question, if you change the structure, the same model will follow instructions much better. In the previous comparison, the model and contract were the same, the only thing that changed was the structure of the input. The reason the model missed the instructions was not because she lacked ability, but because she had no clue as to where the document was and where the request was.

Tools for creating boundaries are delimiters and XML tags. Divider lines and markdown headers show the hierarchy of sections, and tags such as `<document>`, `<instructions>`, and `<question>` name and enclose the type of content. Multiple documents can be separated by tags, including source information such as `<source>`, to reduce article numbers being mixed up.

The principles of order are shared by both guides. Place longer documents at the top and questions at the end. Even if the context window is large, the structure and positioning of the question still affect the quality of the response. When creating input, you first divide the pieces into documents, sources, instructions, examples, and questions, and then stack them in that order.

To summarize, the judgment in this class is condensed into two questions. What is this piece, is the boundary marked, and is the question placed right before writing the answer? If you can answer yes to both of these questions, your input structure is generally stable. Conversely, if the response is wavering, it is best to check these two things first before increasing the instruction sentences. Remember that even for the same contract and the same question, if the structure is different, the results will be different.

callout.label: order to remember
callout.text: Document → Instructions → Examples → Questions. Place long information at the top and questions at the end.

glossary.def: This is a mark that divides the input area. Dividers, titles, and Markdown headers fall into this category and help keep instructions and material from getting mixed up.
This is a method of wrapping the type of content with a name, such as `<document>` and `<instructions>`. Claude guides recommend this in his multi-element prompts.
Claude's guide recommends placing long inputs of 20k tokens or more at the top of the prompt, with questions and instructions below them.
For long contexts, the Gemini documentation explains that it usually performs better to place the question at the end of the prompt, after other contexts.

misconceptions.myth: If the context window is large, it doesn't matter how you place the input.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the window is large, the structure of the input and the location of the question affect the quality of the response. The fact that it goes in and the fact that it is read well are different.
For long entries, the recommended placement is to put the material first and the questions at the end. When the question is placed just before writing the answer, the request becomes clearer.

misconceptions.myth: Tags are decoration to make things look nice.
misconceptions.fact: Tags specify the type of content to reduce confusion between instructions and materials. This structure is used as a clue for the model to read.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The input structure determines the model's reading order.
Divide documents, instructions, examples, and questions into separators and tags.
Place long documents at the top and questions at the end.
Multiple documents are separated by tags, even source metadata.
